title: Hansberry v. Lee (1940)
summary: The earlier judgment could not bind persons whose interests were not adequately represented in the purported class action.
notes:
The holding here is about representation and preclusion. It is not the later constitutional holding concerning judicial enforcement of racially restrictive covenants in Shelley v. Kraemer.

Carl Hansberry (father of playwright Lorraine Hansberry) bought a home in Chicago's Washington Park in 1937; the covenant required signatures of owners of 95 percent of the frontage but only about 54 percent had signed, and the earlier suit, Burke v. Kleiman, had proceeded on a stipulation that 95 percent had signed; Justice Stone wrote for the Court, reversing the Illinois Supreme Court.

sections.Parties: Hansberry and other defendants resisted enforcement of a racially restrictive covenant; neighboring owners sought its enforcement.
sections.Material Facts: The covenant applied to a Chicago neighborhood only if owners representing a specified percentage of frontage had signed. A prior suit had proceeded on a stipulation that the required ninety-five percent had signed, while the later litigation showed a much smaller percentage. The proponents of enforcement claimed that the earlier judgment settled the covenant’s validity for everyone. But owners who wanted the restriction enforced and those who wanted freedom from it had opposing interests.
sections.Procedural History: The Illinois courts treated the prior adjudication as binding on the defendants. The Supreme Court reversed on due-process grounds.
sections.Issue: Could the earlier representative judgment preclude the defendants from disputing the covenant’s effectiveness?
sections.Holding: No. The purported class did not provide adequate representation for persons whose interests opposed those advanced in the earlier suit.
sections.Reasoning: A representative action can bind absent persons when the representatives protect a genuinely shared interest through fair procedure. The formal label of a class cannot overcome an actual conflict about the very obligation being enforced. Owners seeking to establish the restriction could not fairly represent owners seeking to defeat it. The Court therefore refused to make the earlier stipulation conclusive against the later defendants. Its reasoning concerns the legitimacy and limits of representation, rather than simply whether the absent person received actual notice.

learning.why: The earlier judgment could not bind persons whose interests were not adequately represented in the purported class action.

topics.cp-adequate-representation: A prior purported class could not bind persons whose interests opposed those of its representatives.
topics.cp-nonparty-protection: Representation is a limited exception to the ordinary rule against binding nonparties.
topics.cp-class-preclusion: The binding effect of a class judgment depends on adequate representation.
topics.cp-due-process: The decision grounds the adequate-representation requirement in the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
topics.cp-finality: The case limits when a prior judgment may bind persons who were not parties.

mnemonic.rationale: A covenant the neighbours could not enforce
